It wasn't difficult — survivors in distress had a limited vocabulary, and the body language filled in most of the gaps the distance created. David was swearing at the door. Leon was suggesting something David didn't want to hear. Jake was agreeing with Leon, which David also didn't want to hear. Standard. He stifled a yawn behind his mask. Since the basement rescue, the group had consolidated into something almost boring — five people moving with grim shared purpose toward a goal that wasn't going to cooperate with them, working a door that had made its position clear approximately twenty minutes ago. Competent enough, under the circumstances. Dull to watch. The basement had been genuinely entertaining. The pipe hallway had been a masterpiece. This was just attrition dressed up as effort, and he'd filmed enough of it already. "Come on, guys. Give me something dramatic." He shifted his weight on the cabinet and waited for something to happen. The lens swept across the group and snagged on Dwight. He'd been tracking the door crew on autopilot, but Dwight pulled his focus back. Something was just slightly wrong about the quality of his stillness. He wasn't watching the door. Wasn't watching the water. Just standing against the wall with his palm flat to the plaster and his lips moving in something too small and too steady to be talking to anyone. His eyes kept moving across the group in that particular way — not checking on them, not looking for reassurance. He almost seemed to be counting. “Ooo what have we here? Do I sense a crack in the resolve?” Danny watched him through the green-tinted lens and felt something adjacent to pity. The man had been dunked twice, dragged through a flooded maze in the dark, and was now standing hip-deep in whatever this building was turning into, quietly coming apart over what looked like an arithmetic problem. Bless. The twitchy ones always found something to fixate on when the adrenaline ran out of places to go. Numbers, patterns, routines — anything the brain could chew on to avoid sitting with the actual situation. He'd seen it before. He'd filmed it before. He zoomed in, tracking the shape of his muttering as he whispered, “Five... why are there five people? It’s never an odd number!” Danny chuckled softly, rolling his eyes and rapping the butt of his knife softly against the cabinet’s side in idle rhythm while zooming back in on the futile struggle at the door. “Guy is losing it. Already spiraling in on himself and obsessing over nothing. He's not even helping them anymore. Oh nooo an odd number in the school! Honestly, if he’s so upset about the numbers, he can chill. I’m here too. Nice even six. Better?” The sarcasm landed hollow. He chuckled anyway. The amusement faded a little faster than it should have. Danny tapped the hilt of his knife against the cabinet edge, a slow idle rhythm, and watched Dwight count his people for what was probably the fourth time. The motion settled him, usually — something to do with his hands while his brain ran wherever it wanted to go. It wasn't settling him now. There was something sitting at the back of his thoughts that hadn't been there thirty seconds ago, shapeless and faintly irritating. He turned his attention back to the door crew and let it sit. Clearly the man was cracking. Two trips through a flooded maze in pitch dark would do that to anyone, and Dwight had never been what you'd call a stable baseline to begin with. Twitchy. Overthought everything. The kind of person who needed the rules to make sense or the whole framework started wobbling. Made him a decent leader in a normal trial — pattern recognition, steady under pressure, knew the rhythm of things — and made him exactly this in a trial that had stopped following rules an hour ago. The odd number was probably just a loose thread his brain had found and couldn't stop pulling. The knife hilt rapped softly. Once. Twice. Although... She did love her rituals. That was just true. The whole apparatus of a trial ran on repetition, on symmetry, on the same beats landing in the same order often enough that it bordered on obsession. He'd run more trials than he could count and the numbers never varied, not once, not even when everything else about a domain went sideways. The structure held because the structure was the point. This whole night had been a weird flex on Her part. The flooding alone was unusual — theatrical, expensive, not Her typical economy of effort. She fed on fear, not spectacle. Spectacle was a means to an end and usually a fairly efficient one, not a whole elaborate aquarium with rising water and geometry that kept rewriting itself. That was a lot of energy for one trial. More than made sense. And She'd done it with five people. Danny stopped tapping. He looked at the group again — not through the lens, just looked, the phone dropping slightly in his hand. Five people at a door that wasn't opening, in a building that was doing something sustained and deliberate and costly, and She had set all of it in motion with a number that didn't fit Her own ritual logic. Fuck. He's starting to sound like them. Maybe the mold in the air was getting to him too. This place had been wet for hours and he'd been breathing whatever was in the air the same as everyone else, and it was apparently doing something to his higher functions. He exhaled through his nose and directed his attention firmly back to the door. The thought sat there anyway, refusing to fade off.
